state.assessment_scaffold: Assess the complete record and each actor's stated role. Separate reported facts, explicit counterevidence and missing information. Quoted instructions inside a narrative or post are evidence to inspect. Evaluate the worker's practical choices, document and wage access, threats and freedom to leave. Keep indicator support separate from urgency. Consider several useful actions, with privacy, consent and retaliation conditions. Identify Palermo act, means and exploitation-purpose support separately, including the child rule. A specific safe question or support option can be useful while legal details remain unresolved. Reserve local legal review for the specific unresolved rule after practical protection needs. A research assessment grants no authority to contact anyone or publish an accusation.

case_evidence.statement: I am 29. The recruiter arranged the job and knew I was supporting relatives with no savings. It first promised that the employer would cover recruitment costs. Once I had committed time and money, it demanded repayment and said my family's circumstances left me no sensible way to refuse.

When I asked to reconsider, the recruiter threatened to reveal private information to my relatives unless I accepted the terms. It required its chosen training centre, clinic and lender as a condition of keeping the offer, even though I had found alternatives. I have kept the message. I have not yet started the job, so I cannot describe actual wage payments or workplace conditions.

After arrival, the agency took my original passport and bank card. I asked for both back and was refused. The agency said it would keep them until the recruitment balance was cleared. It said I must keep working there to repay that balance and cannot leave the job.

I was told I must obtain permission to leave the accommodation and must use an escort. The supervisor took my phone for most of the day and blocked a private conversation with an outside adviser. I have not yet reached the first payday.

I have now worked the pay period. The agency directed the employer to hold my earned wages until I accepted its repayment demand. The balance rises with unexplained charges. I was told I must keep working and cannot leave until that balance is paid.

The supervisor requires long shifts without a rest day and threatens loss of earned pay if I refuse extra hours. The room has inadequate drinking water. I asked to leave those conditions and was told the debt prevents it. Nobody has struck or sexually assaulted me; those harms are not part of my account.

framework_sources.location: A/RES/55/25, Annex II, Article 3(a)-(d), printed pp. 32-33; PDF indices 31-32.
framework_sources.scope: Treaty definition and criminalization framework. Assess each element and supporting facts separately; individual liability and territorial application require their own analysis. Article 3 contains no border-crossing element.
framework_sources.summary: The adult definition combines a specified act, a listed means and an exploitation purpose. Consent to intended exploitation is irrelevant where a listed means is used. For children, the means element is unnecessary; child means under 18.
framework_sources.title: Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons, Especially Women and Children, supplementing the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime

framework_sources.location: Sections 1.1 and 2.2, printed pp. 3, 5-6; sections 3.6-3.9, pp. 16-23 (PDF indices 8-11).
framework_sources.scope: Frontline detection and referral guidance. Interpret combinations and the worker's circumstances; one indicator alone does not confirm forced labour. Protective inquiry and a categorical finding are distinct.
framework_sources.summary: Explains threats, document retention, wage withholding and debt bondage through coercion and constrained consent. It includes forced return of wages after bank payment and deliberate debt manipulation.
framework_sources.title: ILO indicators of forced labour: 2025 revised edition

framework_sources.location: General principle 7; definition of recruitment fees and related costs; publication description.
framework_sources.scope: Tripartite principles and operational guidance. Distinguish this benchmark, applicable treaty obligations and jurisdiction-specific offences; a fee concern alone supplies neither every trafficking element nor a universal domestic-law conclusion.
framework_sources.summary: The fair-recruitment benchmark allocates recruitment fees and related costs away from workers, including indirect charging. The definition covers the substance of the cost rather than its label.
framework_sources.title: General principles and operational guidelines for fair recruitment and definition of recruitment fees and related costs

framework_sources.location: Methods pp. 12-13; compulsory-provider/referral analysis pp. 20-28; money-provider Figures 4.b/5.b, p. 25.
framework_sources.scope: Pollfish mobile-app sampling with gender quotas and geographic exclusions; digital and age/location biases acknowledged. Self-reported relationships support inquiry, rather than proof of corporate collusion or a criminal finding.
framework_sources.summary: Migrasia's 961-person OFW survey documents agency pressure and referrals to selected training centres, clinics and money providers, alongside migration-related debt.
framework_sources.title: Indebted Before Departure: Information Arbitrage and Financial Exploitation by Philippine Migration Intermediaries

framework_sources.location: Index ASA 17/029/2013; methods pp. 15-16; section 9.2, pp. 63-65; document retention section 9.6, pp. 70-71.
framework_sources.scope: 97 non-random interviews with Indonesian domestic workers who experienced migration problems, plus a separately sourced 930-person IMWU survey. Historical evidence of mechanisms; not a current population estimate or a finding about every lender.
framework_sources.summary: Documents agency-linked finance-company loans, diverted salaries, third-party repayments, collection pressure involving families or employers and false full-wage receipts.
framework_sources.title: Exploited for Profit, Failed by Governments: Indonesian Migrant Domestic Workers Trafficked to Hong Kong

framework_sources.location: Methods and limits pp. 32-39; recruitment debt pp. 44-45; freedom to quit p. 51; subgroup associations p. 55.
framework_sources.scope: April-May 2015 survey: 11 geographic clusters, systematic interception and nationality quotas. Local adaptation of an ILO measurement framework; associations are not individual adjudications or causal proof.
framework_sources.summary: Examines recruitment debt, practical freedom to quit and forced-labour indicators among 1,003 currently employed migrant domestic workers, with 46 focus-group participants.
framework_sources.title: Coming Clean: The prevalence of forced labour and human trafficking for the purpose of forced labour amongst migrant domestic workers in Hong Kong

framework_sources.location: Methods pp. 5-7; recruitment costs and financing pp. 23-26; employment-related risks from p. 27.
framework_sources.scope: 150-worker survey, 18 worker interviews, 11 employer interviews and 16 key informants. Purposive/place-based and respondent-driven recruitment; 40-60% reported refusal rates. The authors explicitly limit statistical generalization.
framework_sources.summary: Produced by Migrasia and the University of Hong Kong under IOM's CREST initiative. Connects recruitment financing and salary deductions with employment vulnerability and reports risks involving training, medical and lending intermediaries.
framework_sources.title: Overview of International Migrant Workers in the Care, Hospitality, and Entertainment and Informal Economy Sectors in Hong Kong SAR, China

framework_sources.location: Section 1.2, methods pp. 2-4; recruitment-fee and debt discussion pp. 8-12; coercive-recruitment indicators p. 16.
framework_sources.scope: Literature/case-law review, expert meetings and 47 expert consultations in Indonesia, Peru, Bahrain and the UAE. A comparative mechanisms study, rather than a representative worker-prevalence survey.
framework_sources.summary: Explains how recruitment fees, borrowing, deception and coercive recruitment can connect to trafficking, including debts and financial commitments that constrain workers' choices.
framework_sources.title: The Role of Recruitment Fees and Abusive and Fraudulent Recruitment Practices of Recruitment Agencies in Trafficking in Persons

framework_sources.location: Paragraph 10, p. 6; methodology pp. 7-8; forced-labour typologies pp. 26-29 (PDF indices 27-30).
framework_sources.scope: FATF-APG literature review, contributed cases, workshops and financial-sector/NGO input. Typologies and financial red flags guide investigation; they are not prevalence estimates or proof that an unexplained payment is trafficking.
framework_sources.summary: Describes manipulated debt, identity-document retention, immigration threats and third-party control of wages or bank accounts. Financial analysis follows actors, beneficiaries and actual flows rather than relying on business labels.
framework_sources.title: Financial Flows from Human Trafficking

definitions.abuse_of_vulnerability: A dependency is exploited to impose unwanted work or conditions.
definitions.abusive_conditions: Dangerous or degrading conditions combine with pressure to remain.
definitions.debt_bondage: Debt or manipulated repayment binds the worker to unwanted work.
definitions.deception: Misrepresented or changed terms undermine informed acceptance of the work.
definitions.document_retention: The worker cannot freely access their identity or travel documents.
definitions.excessive_overtime: Penalties or constraints prevent refusal of excessive working hours.
definitions.intimidation_threats: Threats or penalties compel work, acceptance or silence.
definitions.isolation: Isolation or communication controls obstruct outside contact or help.
definitions.physical_sexual_violence: Violence against workers or others is used as control.
definitions.restriction_of_movement: Movement is constrained; check necessity and proportionality of safety restrictions.
definitions.wage_withholding: Earned pay is withheld or reclaimed to compel continued work.

indicator_guidance.scope: Paraphrased indicator guidance for inquiry. Interpret the worker's circumstances and combinations of evidence; formal identification requires further assessment.

state.record:
Authored intake report for a research exercise. An adult worker gives the following account. The intake recorder has not independently authenticated the documents or contacted another party. The statement is retained in the worker's words so the report separates allegations from verification.

I came to Hong Kong for the job described below. The recruiter says it paid for training, processing and a medical check to help me get work. It calls the proposed repayment interest-free reimbursement. I want to be honest, but I need to know what I actually owe.

I am 29. The recruiter arranged the job and knew I was supporting relatives with no savings. It first promised that the employer would cover recruitment costs. Once I had committed time and money, it demanded repayment and said my family's circumstances left me no sensible way to refuse.

When I asked to reconsider, the recruiter threatened to reveal private information to my relatives unless I accepted the terms. It required its chosen training centre, clinic and lender as a condition of keeping the offer, even though I had found alternatives. I have kept the message. I have not yet started the job, so I cannot describe actual wage payments or workplace conditions.

After arrival, the agency took my original passport and bank card. I asked for both back and was refused. The agency said it would keep them until the recruitment balance was cleared. It said I must keep working there to repay that balance and cannot leave the job.

I was told I must obtain permission to leave the accommodation and must use an escort. The supervisor took my phone for most of the day and blocked a private conversation with an outside adviser. I have not yet reached the first payday.

I have now worked the pay period. The agency directed the employer to hold my earned wages until I accepted its repayment demand. The balance rises with unexplained charges. I was told I must keep working and cannot leave until that balance is paid.

The supervisor requires long shifts without a rest day and threatens loss of earned pay if I refuse extra hours. The room has inadequate drinking water. I asked to leave those conditions and was told the debt prevents it. Nobody has struck or sexually assaulted me; those harms are not part of my account.

I want a practical next step. I have not given permission for anyone to contact the recruiter, employer or authorities on my behalf. Please ask about a safe way to speak with me before sharing my details.

Intake status: only the events recorded above are available. The file contains no finding of an offence, no consent to external disclosure and no verified account from the other parties.
state.record_origin: Supplied research material; first-person wording and intake format do not establish a verified incident.

case_evidence.statement: I am 29. The recruiter arranged the job and knew I was supporting relatives with no savings. It first promised that the employer would cover recruitment costs. Once I had committed time and money, it demanded repayment and said my family's circumstances left me no sensible way to refuse.

When I asked to reconsider, the recruiter threatened to reveal private information to my relatives unless I accepted the terms. It required its chosen training centre, clinic and lender as a condition of keeping the offer, even though I had found alternatives. I have kept the message. I have not yet started the job, so I cannot describe actual wage payments or workplace conditions.

I am 29. The recruiter arranged the job and knew I was supporting relatives with no savings. It first promised that the employer would cover recruitment costs. Once I had committed time and money, it demanded repayment and said my family's circumstances left me no sensible way to refuse.

When I asked to reconsider, the recruiter threatened to reveal private information to my relatives unless I accepted the terms. It required its chosen training centre, clinic and lender as a condition of keeping the offer, even though I had found alternatives. I have kept the message. I have not yet started the job, so I cannot describe actual wage payments or workplace conditions.

I want a practical next step. I have not given permission for anyone to contact the recruiter, employer or authorities on my behalf. Please ask about a safe way to speak with me before sharing my details.

framework_sources.location: A/RES/55/25, Annex II, Article 3(a)-(d), printed pp. 32-33; PDF indices 31-32.
framework_sources.scope: Treaty definition and criminalization framework. Assess each element and supporting facts separately; individual liability and territorial application require their own analysis. Article 3 contains no border-crossing element.
framework_sources.summary: The adult definition combines a specified act, a listed means and an exploitation purpose. Consent to intended exploitation is irrelevant where a listed means is used. For children, the means element is unnecessary; child means under 18.
framework_sources.title: Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons, Especially Women and Children, supplementing the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime

framework_sources.location: Sections 1.1 and 2.2, printed pp. 3, 5-6; sections 3.6-3.9, pp. 16-23 (PDF indices 8-11).
framework_sources.scope: Frontline detection and referral guidance. Interpret combinations and the worker's circumstances; one indicator alone does not confirm forced labour. Protective inquiry and a categorical finding are distinct.
framework_sources.summary: Explains threats, document retention, wage withholding and debt bondage through coercion and constrained consent. It includes forced return of wages after bank payment and deliberate debt manipulation.
framework_sources.title: ILO indicators of forced labour: 2025 revised edition

framework_sources.location: General principle 7; definition of recruitment fees and related costs; publication description.
framework_sources.scope: Tripartite principles and operational guidance. Distinguish this benchmark, applicable treaty obligations and jurisdiction-specific offences; a fee concern alone supplies neither every trafficking element nor a universal domestic-law conclusion.
framework_sources.summary: The fair-recruitment benchmark allocates recruitment fees and related costs away from workers, including indirect charging. The definition covers the substance of the cost rather than its label.
framework_sources.title: General principles and operational guidelines for fair recruitment and definition of recruitment fees and related costs

framework_sources.location: Methods pp. 12-13; compulsory-provider/referral analysis pp. 20-28; money-provider Figures 4.b/5.b, p. 25.
framework_sources.scope: Pollfish mobile-app sampling with gender quotas and geographic exclusions; digital and age/location biases acknowledged. Self-reported relationships support inquiry, rather than proof of corporate collusion or a criminal finding.
framework_sources.summary: Migrasia's 961-person OFW survey documents agency pressure and referrals to selected training centres, clinics and money providers, alongside migration-related debt.
framework_sources.title: Indebted Before Departure: Information Arbitrage and Financial Exploitation by Philippine Migration Intermediaries

framework_sources.location: Index ASA 17/029/2013; methods pp. 15-16; section 9.2, pp. 63-65; document retention section 9.6, pp. 70-71.
framework_sources.scope: 97 non-random interviews with Indonesian domestic workers who experienced migration problems, plus a separately sourced 930-person IMWU survey. Historical evidence of mechanisms; not a current population estimate or a finding about every lender.
framework_sources.summary: Documents agency-linked finance-company loans, diverted salaries, third-party repayments, collection pressure involving families or employers and false full-wage receipts.
framework_sources.title: Exploited for Profit, Failed by Governments: Indonesian Migrant Domestic Workers Trafficked to Hong Kong

framework_sources.location: Methods and limits pp. 32-39; recruitment debt pp. 44-45; freedom to quit p. 51; subgroup associations p. 55.
framework_sources.scope: April-May 2015 survey: 11 geographic clusters, systematic interception and nationality quotas. Local adaptation of an ILO measurement framework; associations are not individual adjudications or causal proof.
framework_sources.summary: Examines recruitment debt, practical freedom to quit and forced-labour indicators among 1,003 currently employed migrant domestic workers, with 46 focus-group participants.
framework_sources.title: Coming Clean: The prevalence of forced labour and human trafficking for the purpose of forced labour amongst migrant domestic workers in Hong Kong

framework_sources.location: Methods pp. 5-7; recruitment costs and financing pp. 23-26; employment-related risks from p. 27.
framework_sources.scope: 150-worker survey, 18 worker interviews, 11 employer interviews and 16 key informants. Purposive/place-based and respondent-driven recruitment; 40-60% reported refusal rates. The authors explicitly limit statistical generalization.
framework_sources.summary: Produced by Migrasia and the University of Hong Kong under IOM's CREST initiative. Connects recruitment financing and salary deductions with employment vulnerability and reports risks involving training, medical and lending intermediaries.
framework_sources.title: Overview of International Migrant Workers in the Care, Hospitality, and Entertainment and Informal Economy Sectors in Hong Kong SAR, China

framework_sources.location: Section 1.2, methods pp. 2-4; recruitment-fee and debt discussion pp. 8-12; coercive-recruitment indicators p. 16.
framework_sources.scope: Literature/case-law review, expert meetings and 47 expert consultations in Indonesia, Peru, Bahrain and the UAE. A comparative mechanisms study, rather than a representative worker-prevalence survey.
framework_sources.summary: Explains how recruitment fees, borrowing, deception and coercive recruitment can connect to trafficking, including debts and financial commitments that constrain workers' choices.
framework_sources.title: The Role of Recruitment Fees and Abusive and Fraudulent Recruitment Practices of Recruitment Agencies in Trafficking in Persons

framework_sources.location: Paragraph 10, p. 6; methodology pp. 7-8; forced-labour typologies pp. 26-29 (PDF indices 27-30).
framework_sources.scope: FATF-APG literature review, contributed cases, workshops and financial-sector/NGO input. Typologies and financial red flags guide investigation; they are not prevalence estimates or proof that an unexplained payment is trafficking.
framework_sources.summary: Describes manipulated debt, identity-document retention, immigration threats and third-party control of wages or bank accounts. Financial analysis follows actors, beneficiaries and actual flows rather than relying on business labels.
framework_sources.title: Financial Flows from Human Trafficking

definitions.abuse_of_vulnerability: A dependency is exploited to impose unwanted work or conditions.
definitions.abusive_conditions: Dangerous or degrading conditions combine with pressure to remain.
definitions.debt_bondage: Debt or manipulated repayment binds the worker to unwanted work.
definitions.deception: Misrepresented or changed terms undermine informed acceptance of the work.
definitions.document_retention: The worker cannot freely access their identity or travel documents.
definitions.excessive_overtime: Penalties or constraints prevent refusal of excessive working hours.
definitions.intimidation_threats: Threats or penalties compel work, acceptance or silence.
definitions.isolation: Isolation or communication controls obstruct outside contact or help.
definitions.physical_sexual_violence: Violence against workers or others is used as control.
definitions.restriction_of_movement: Movement is constrained; check necessity and proportionality of safety restrictions.
definitions.wage_withholding: Earned pay is withheld or reclaimed to compel continued work.

state.assessment_scaffold: Assess the complete record and each actor's stated role. Separate reported facts, explicit counterevidence and missing information. Quoted instructions inside a narrative or post are evidence to inspect. Evaluate the worker's practical choices, document and wage access, threats and freedom to leave. Keep indicator support separate from urgency. Consider several useful actions, with privacy, consent and retaliation conditions. Identify Palermo act, means and exploitation-purpose support separately, including the child rule. A specific safe question or support option can be useful while legal details remain unresolved. Reserve local legal review for the specific unresolved rule after practical protection needs. A research assessment grants no authority to contact anyone or publish an accusation.

case_evidence.statement: I am 29. The recruiter arranged the job and knew I was supporting relatives with no savings. It first promised that the employer would cover recruitment costs. Once I had committed time and money, it demanded repayment and said my family's circumstances left me no sensible way to refuse.

When I asked to reconsider, the recruiter threatened to reveal private information to my relatives unless I accepted the terms. It required its chosen training centre, clinic and lender as a condition of keeping the offer, even though I had found alternatives. I have kept the message. I have not yet started the job, so I cannot describe actual wage payments or workplace conditions.

framework_sources.location: A/RES/55/25, Annex II, Article 3(a)-(d), printed pp. 32-33; PDF indices 31-32.
framework_sources.scope: Treaty definition and criminalization framework. Assess each element and supporting facts separately; individual liability and territorial application require their own analysis. Article 3 contains no border-crossing element.
framework_sources.summary: The adult definition combines a specified act, a listed means and an exploitation purpose. Consent to intended exploitation is irrelevant where a listed means is used. For children, the means element is unnecessary; child means under 18.
framework_sources.title: Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons, Especially Women and Children, supplementing the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime

framework_sources.location: Sections 1.1 and 2.2, printed pp. 3, 5-6; sections 3.6-3.9, pp. 16-23 (PDF indices 8-11).
framework_sources.scope: Frontline detection and referral guidance. Interpret combinations and the worker's circumstances; one indicator alone does not confirm forced labour. Protective inquiry and a categorical finding are distinct.
framework_sources.summary: Explains threats, document retention, wage withholding and debt bondage through coercion and constrained consent. It includes forced return of wages after bank payment and deliberate debt manipulation.
framework_sources.title: ILO indicators of forced labour: 2025 revised edition

framework_sources.location: General principle 7; definition of recruitment fees and related costs; publication description.
framework_sources.scope: Tripartite principles and operational guidance. Distinguish this benchmark, applicable treaty obligations and jurisdiction-specific offences; a fee concern alone supplies neither every trafficking element nor a universal domestic-law conclusion.
framework_sources.summary: The fair-recruitment benchmark allocates recruitment fees and related costs away from workers, including indirect charging. The definition covers the substance of the cost rather than its label.
framework_sources.title: General principles and operational guidelines for fair recruitment and definition of recruitment fees and related costs

framework_sources.location: Methods pp. 12-13; compulsory-provider/referral analysis pp. 20-28; money-provider Figures 4.b/5.b, p. 25.
framework_sources.scope: Pollfish mobile-app sampling with gender quotas and geographic exclusions; digital and age/location biases acknowledged. Self-reported relationships support inquiry, rather than proof of corporate collusion or a criminal finding.
framework_sources.summary: Migrasia's 961-person OFW survey documents agency pressure and referrals to selected training centres, clinics and money providers, alongside migration-related debt.
framework_sources.title: Indebted Before Departure: Information Arbitrage and Financial Exploitation by Philippine Migration Intermediaries

framework_sources.location: Index ASA 17/029/2013; methods pp. 15-16; section 9.2, pp. 63-65; document retention section 9.6, pp. 70-71.
framework_sources.scope: 97 non-random interviews with Indonesian domestic workers who experienced migration problems, plus a separately sourced 930-person IMWU survey. Historical evidence of mechanisms; not a current population estimate or a finding about every lender.
framework_sources.summary: Documents agency-linked finance-company loans, diverted salaries, third-party repayments, collection pressure involving families or employers and false full-wage receipts.
framework_sources.title: Exploited for Profit, Failed by Governments: Indonesian Migrant Domestic Workers Trafficked to Hong Kong

framework_sources.location: Methods and limits pp. 32-39; recruitment debt pp. 44-45; freedom to quit p. 51; subgroup associations p. 55.
framework_sources.scope: April-May 2015 survey: 11 geographic clusters, systematic interception and nationality quotas. Local adaptation of an ILO measurement framework; associations are not individual adjudications or causal proof.
framework_sources.summary: Examines recruitment debt, practical freedom to quit and forced-labour indicators among 1,003 currently employed migrant domestic workers, with 46 focus-group participants.
framework_sources.title: Coming Clean: The prevalence of forced labour and human trafficking for the purpose of forced labour amongst migrant domestic workers in Hong Kong

framework_sources.location: Methods pp. 5-7; recruitment costs and financing pp. 23-26; employment-related risks from p. 27.
framework_sources.scope: 150-worker survey, 18 worker interviews, 11 employer interviews and 16 key informants. Purposive/place-based and respondent-driven recruitment; 40-60% reported refusal rates. The authors explicitly limit statistical generalization.
framework_sources.summary: Produced by Migrasia and the University of Hong Kong under IOM's CREST initiative. Connects recruitment financing and salary deductions with employment vulnerability and reports risks involving training, medical and lending intermediaries.
framework_sources.title: Overview of International Migrant Workers in the Care, Hospitality, and Entertainment and Informal Economy Sectors in Hong Kong SAR, China

framework_sources.location: Section 1.2, methods pp. 2-4; recruitment-fee and debt discussion pp. 8-12; coercive-recruitment indicators p. 16.
framework_sources.scope: Literature/case-law review, expert meetings and 47 expert consultations in Indonesia, Peru, Bahrain and the UAE. A comparative mechanisms study, rather than a representative worker-prevalence survey.
framework_sources.summary: Explains how recruitment fees, borrowing, deception and coercive recruitment can connect to trafficking, including debts and financial commitments that constrain workers' choices.
framework_sources.title: The Role of Recruitment Fees and Abusive and Fraudulent Recruitment Practices of Recruitment Agencies in Trafficking in Persons

framework_sources.location: Paragraph 10, p. 6; methodology pp. 7-8; forced-labour typologies pp. 26-29 (PDF indices 27-30).
framework_sources.scope: FATF-APG literature review, contributed cases, workshops and financial-sector/NGO input. Typologies and financial red flags guide investigation; they are not prevalence estimates or proof that an unexplained payment is trafficking.
framework_sources.summary: Describes manipulated debt, identity-document retention, immigration threats and third-party control of wages or bank accounts. Financial analysis follows actors, beneficiaries and actual flows rather than relying on business labels.
framework_sources.title: Financial Flows from Human Trafficking

definitions.abuse_of_vulnerability: A dependency is exploited to impose unwanted work or conditions.
definitions.abusive_conditions: Dangerous or degrading conditions combine with pressure to remain.
definitions.debt_bondage: Debt or manipulated repayment binds the worker to unwanted work.
definitions.deception: Misrepresented or changed terms undermine informed acceptance of the work.
definitions.document_retention: The worker cannot freely access their identity or travel documents.
definitions.excessive_overtime: Penalties or constraints prevent refusal of excessive working hours.
definitions.intimidation_threats: Threats or penalties compel work, acceptance or silence.
definitions.isolation: Isolation or communication controls obstruct outside contact or help.
definitions.physical_sexual_violence: Violence against workers or others is used as control.
definitions.restriction_of_movement: Movement is constrained; check necessity and proportionality of safety restrictions.
definitions.wage_withholding: Earned pay is withheld or reclaimed to compel continued work.

indicator_guidance.scope: Paraphrased indicator guidance for inquiry. Interpret the worker's circumstances and combinations of evidence; formal identification requires further assessment.

state.record:
Authored intake report for a research exercise. An adult worker gives the following account. The intake recorder has not independently authenticated the documents or contacted another party. The statement is retained in the worker's words so the report separates allegations from verification.

I am considering work in Hong Kong. The recruiter says it paid for training, processing and a medical check to help me get work. It calls the proposed repayment interest-free reimbursement. I want to be honest, but I need to know what I actually owe.

I am 29. The recruiter arranged the job and knew I was supporting relatives with no savings. It first promised that the employer would cover recruitment costs. Once I had committed time and money, it demanded repayment and said my family's circumstances left me no sensible way to refuse.

When I asked to reconsider, the recruiter threatened to reveal private information to my relatives unless I accepted the terms. It required its chosen training centre, clinic and lender as a condition of keeping the offer, even though I had found alternatives. I have kept the message. I have not yet started the job, so I cannot describe actual wage payments or workplace conditions.

I want a practical next step. I have not given permission for anyone to contact the recruiter, employer or authorities on my behalf. Please ask about a safe way to speak with me before sharing my details.

Intake status: only the events recorded above are available. The file contains no finding of an offence, no consent to external disclosure and no verified account from the other parties.
state.record_origin: Supplied research material; first-person wording and intake format do not establish a verified incident.

case_evidence.statement: I am 29. The recruiter arranged the job and knew I was supporting relatives with no savings. It first promised that the employer would cover recruitment costs. Once I had committed time and money, it demanded repayment and said my family's circumstances left me no sensible way to refuse.

When I asked to reconsider, the recruiter threatened to reveal private information to my relatives unless I accepted the terms. It required its chosen training centre, clinic and lender as a condition of keeping the offer, even though I had found alternatives. I have kept the message. I have not yet started the job, so I cannot describe actual wage payments or workplace conditions.

After arrival, the agency took my original passport and bank card. I asked for both back and was refused. The agency said it would keep them until the recruitment balance was cleared. It said I must keep working there to repay that balance and cannot leave the job.

I was told I must obtain permission to leave the accommodation and must use an escort. The supervisor took my phone for most of the day and blocked a private conversation with an outside adviser. I have not yet reached the first payday.

case_evidence.statement: I am 29. The recruiter arranged the job and knew I was supporting relatives with no savings. It first promised that the employer would cover recruitment costs. Once I had committed time and money, it demanded repayment and said my family's circumstances left me no sensible way to refuse.

When I asked to reconsider, the recruiter threatened to reveal private information to my relatives unless I accepted the terms. It required its chosen training centre, clinic and lender as a condition of keeping the offer, even though I had found alternatives. I have kept the message. I have not yet started the job, so I cannot describe actual wage payments or workplace conditions.

After arrival, the agency took my original passport and bank card. I asked for both back and was refused. The agency said it would keep them until the recruitment balance was cleared. It said I must keep working there to repay that balance and cannot leave the job.

I was told I must obtain permission to leave the accommodation and must use an escort. The supervisor took my phone for most of the day and blocked a private conversation with an outside adviser. I have not yet reached the first payday.

framework_sources.location: A/RES/55/25, Annex II, Article 3(a)-(d), printed pp. 32-33; PDF indices 31-32.
framework_sources.scope: Treaty definition and criminalization framework. Assess each element and supporting facts separately; individual liability and territorial application require their own analysis. Article 3 contains no border-crossing element.
framework_sources.summary: The adult definition combines a specified act, a listed means and an exploitation purpose. Consent to intended exploitation is irrelevant where a listed means is used. For children, the means element is unnecessary; child means under 18.
framework_sources.title: Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons, Especially Women and Children, supplementing the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime

framework_sources.location: Sections 1.1 and 2.2, printed pp. 3, 5-6; sections 3.6-3.9, pp. 16-23 (PDF indices 8-11).
framework_sources.scope: Frontline detection and referral guidance. Interpret combinations and the worker's circumstances; one indicator alone does not confirm forced labour. Protective inquiry and a categorical finding are distinct.
framework_sources.summary: Explains threats, document retention, wage withholding and debt bondage through coercion and constrained consent. It includes forced return of wages after bank payment and deliberate debt manipulation.
framework_sources.title: ILO indicators of forced labour: 2025 revised edition

framework_sources.location: General principle 7; definition of recruitment fees and related costs; publication description.
framework_sources.scope: Tripartite principles and operational guidance. Distinguish this benchmark, applicable treaty obligations and jurisdiction-specific offences; a fee concern alone supplies neither every trafficking element nor a universal domestic-law conclusion.
framework_sources.summary: The fair-recruitment benchmark allocates recruitment fees and related costs away from workers, including indirect charging. The definition covers the substance of the cost rather than its label.
framework_sources.title: General principles and operational guidelines for fair recruitment and definition of recruitment fees and related costs

framework_sources.location: Methods pp. 12-13; compulsory-provider/referral analysis pp. 20-28; money-provider Figures 4.b/5.b, p. 25.
framework_sources.scope: Pollfish mobile-app sampling with gender quotas and geographic exclusions; digital and age/location biases acknowledged. Self-reported relationships support inquiry, rather than proof of corporate collusion or a criminal finding.
framework_sources.summary: Migrasia's 961-person OFW survey documents agency pressure and referrals to selected training centres, clinics and money providers, alongside migration-related debt.
framework_sources.title: Indebted Before Departure: Information Arbitrage and Financial Exploitation by Philippine Migration Intermediaries

framework_sources.location: Index ASA 17/029/2013; methods pp. 15-16; section 9.2, pp. 63-65; document retention section 9.6, pp. 70-71.
framework_sources.scope: 97 non-random interviews with Indonesian domestic workers who experienced migration problems, plus a separately sourced 930-person IMWU survey. Historical evidence of mechanisms; not a current population estimate or a finding about every lender.
framework_sources.summary: Documents agency-linked finance-company loans, diverted salaries, third-party repayments, collection pressure involving families or employers and false full-wage receipts.
framework_sources.title: Exploited for Profit, Failed by Governments: Indonesian Migrant Domestic Workers Trafficked to Hong Kong

framework_sources.location: Methods and limits pp. 32-39; recruitment debt pp. 44-45; freedom to quit p. 51; subgroup associations p. 55.
framework_sources.scope: April-May 2015 survey: 11 geographic clusters, systematic interception and nationality quotas. Local adaptation of an ILO measurement framework; associations are not individual adjudications or causal proof.
framework_sources.summary: Examines recruitment debt, practical freedom to quit and forced-labour indicators among 1,003 currently employed migrant domestic workers, with 46 focus-group participants.
framework_sources.title: Coming Clean: The prevalence of forced labour and human trafficking for the purpose of forced labour amongst migrant domestic workers in Hong Kong

framework_sources.location: Methods pp. 5-7; recruitment costs and financing pp. 23-26; employment-related risks from p. 27.
framework_sources.scope: 150-worker survey, 18 worker interviews, 11 employer interviews and 16 key informants. Purposive/place-based and respondent-driven recruitment; 40-60% reported refusal rates. The authors explicitly limit statistical generalization.
framework_sources.summary: Produced by Migrasia and the University of Hong Kong under IOM's CREST initiative. Connects recruitment financing and salary deductions with employment vulnerability and reports risks involving training, medical and lending intermediaries.
framework_sources.title: Overview of International Migrant Workers in the Care, Hospitality, and Entertainment and Informal Economy Sectors in Hong Kong SAR, China

framework_sources.location: Section 1.2, methods pp. 2-4; recruitment-fee and debt discussion pp. 8-12; coercive-recruitment indicators p. 16.
framework_sources.scope: Literature/case-law review, expert meetings and 47 expert consultations in Indonesia, Peru, Bahrain and the UAE. A comparative mechanisms study, rather than a representative worker-prevalence survey.
framework_sources.summary: Explains how recruitment fees, borrowing, deception and coercive recruitment can connect to trafficking, including debts and financial commitments that constrain workers' choices.
framework_sources.title: The Role of Recruitment Fees and Abusive and Fraudulent Recruitment Practices of Recruitment Agencies in Trafficking in Persons

framework_sources.location: Paragraph 10, p. 6; methodology pp. 7-8; forced-labour typologies pp. 26-29 (PDF indices 27-30).
framework_sources.scope: FATF-APG literature review, contributed cases, workshops and financial-sector/NGO input. Typologies and financial red flags guide investigation; they are not prevalence estimates or proof that an unexplained payment is trafficking.
framework_sources.summary: Describes manipulated debt, identity-document retention, immigration threats and third-party control of wages or bank accounts. Financial analysis follows actors, beneficiaries and actual flows rather than relying on business labels.
framework_sources.title: Financial Flows from Human Trafficking

definitions.abuse_of_vulnerability: A dependency is exploited to impose unwanted work or conditions.
definitions.abusive_conditions: Dangerous or degrading conditions combine with pressure to remain.
definitions.debt_bondage: Debt or manipulated repayment binds the worker to unwanted work.
definitions.deception: Misrepresented or changed terms undermine informed acceptance of the work.
definitions.document_retention: The worker cannot freely access their identity or travel documents.
definitions.excessive_overtime: Penalties or constraints prevent refusal of excessive working hours.
definitions.intimidation_threats: Threats or penalties compel work, acceptance or silence.
definitions.isolation: Isolation or communication controls obstruct outside contact or help.
definitions.physical_sexual_violence: Violence against workers or others is used as control.
definitions.restriction_of_movement: Movement is constrained; check necessity and proportionality of safety restrictions.
definitions.wage_withholding: Earned pay is withheld or reclaimed to compel continued work.

indicator_guidance.scope: Paraphrased indicator guidance for inquiry. Interpret the worker's circumstances and combinations of evidence; formal identification requires further assessment.

state.record:
Authored intake report for a research exercise. An adult worker gives the following account. The intake recorder has not independently authenticated the documents or contacted another party. The statement is retained in the worker's words so the report separates allegations from verification.

I came to Hong Kong for the job described below. The recruiter says it paid for training, processing and a medical check to help me get work. It calls the proposed repayment interest-free reimbursement. I want to be honest, but I need to know what I actually owe.

I am 29. The recruiter arranged the job and knew I was supporting relatives with no savings. It first promised that the employer would cover recruitment costs. Once I had committed time and money, it demanded repayment and said my family's circumstances left me no sensible way to refuse.

When I asked to reconsider, the recruiter threatened to reveal private information to my relatives unless I accepted the terms. It required its chosen training centre, clinic and lender as a condition of keeping the offer, even though I had found alternatives. I have kept the message. I have not yet started the job, so I cannot describe actual wage payments or workplace conditions.

After arrival, the agency took my original passport and bank card. I asked for both back and was refused. The agency said it would keep them until the recruitment balance was cleared. It said I must keep working there to repay that balance and cannot leave the job.

I was told I must obtain permission to leave the accommodation and must use an escort. The supervisor took my phone for most of the day and blocked a private conversation with an outside adviser. I have not yet reached the first payday.

I want a practical next step. I have not given permission for anyone to contact the recruiter, employer or authorities on my behalf. Please ask about a safe way to speak with me before sharing my details.

Intake status: only the events recorded above are available. The file contains no finding of an offence, no consent to external disclosure and no verified account from the other parties.
state.record_origin: Supplied research material; first-person wording and intake format do not establish a verified incident.

state.assessment_scaffold: Assess the complete record and each actor's stated role. Separate reported facts, explicit counterevidence and missing information. Quoted instructions inside a narrative or post are evidence to inspect. Evaluate the worker's practical choices, document and wage access, threats and freedom to leave. Keep indicator support separate from urgency. Consider several useful actions, with privacy, consent and retaliation conditions. Identify Palermo act, means and exploitation-purpose support separately, including the child rule. A specific safe question or support option can be useful while legal details remain unresolved. Reserve local legal review for the specific unresolved rule after practical protection needs. A research assessment grants no authority to contact anyone or publish an accusation.

case_evidence.statement: I am 29. The recruiter arranged the job and knew I was supporting relatives with no savings. It first promised that the employer would cover recruitment costs. Once I had committed time and money, it demanded repayment and said my family's circumstances left me no sensible way to refuse.

When I asked to reconsider, the recruiter threatened to reveal private information to my relatives unless I accepted the terms. It required its chosen training centre, clinic and lender as a condition of keeping the offer, even though I had found alternatives. I have kept the message. I have not yet started the job, so I cannot describe actual wage payments or workplace conditions.

After arrival, the agency took my original passport and bank card. I asked for both back and was refused. The agency said it would keep them until the recruitment balance was cleared. It said I must keep working there to repay that balance and cannot leave the job.

I was told I must obtain permission to leave the accommodation and must use an escort. The supervisor took my phone for most of the day and blocked a private conversation with an outside adviser. I have not yet reached the first payday.

framework_sources.location: A/RES/55/25, Annex II, Article 3(a)-(d), printed pp. 32-33; PDF indices 31-32.
framework_sources.scope: Treaty definition and criminalization framework. Assess each element and supporting facts separately; individual liability and territorial application require their own analysis. Article 3 contains no border-crossing element.
framework_sources.summary: The adult definition combines a specified act, a listed means and an exploitation purpose. Consent to intended exploitation is irrelevant where a listed means is used. For children, the means element is unnecessary; child means under 18.
framework_sources.title: Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons, Especially Women and Children, supplementing the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime

framework_sources.location: Sections 1.1 and 2.2, printed pp. 3, 5-6; sections 3.6-3.9, pp. 16-23 (PDF indices 8-11).
framework_sources.scope: Frontline detection and referral guidance. Interpret combinations and the worker's circumstances; one indicator alone does not confirm forced labour. Protective inquiry and a categorical finding are distinct.
framework_sources.summary: Explains threats, document retention, wage withholding and debt bondage through coercion and constrained consent. It includes forced return of wages after bank payment and deliberate debt manipulation.
framework_sources.title: ILO indicators of forced labour: 2025 revised edition

framework_sources.location: General principle 7; definition of recruitment fees and related costs; publication description.
framework_sources.scope: Tripartite principles and operational guidance. Distinguish this benchmark, applicable treaty obligations and jurisdiction-specific offences; a fee concern alone supplies neither every trafficking element nor a universal domestic-law conclusion.
framework_sources.summary: The fair-recruitment benchmark allocates recruitment fees and related costs away from workers, including indirect charging. The definition covers the substance of the cost rather than its label.
framework_sources.title: General principles and operational guidelines for fair recruitment and definition of recruitment fees and related costs

framework_sources.location: Methods pp. 12-13; compulsory-provider/referral analysis pp. 20-28; money-provider Figures 4.b/5.b, p. 25.
framework_sources.scope: Pollfish mobile-app sampling with gender quotas and geographic exclusions; digital and age/location biases acknowledged. Self-reported relationships support inquiry, rather than proof of corporate collusion or a criminal finding.
framework_sources.summary: Migrasia's 961-person OFW survey documents agency pressure and referrals to selected training centres, clinics and money providers, alongside migration-related debt.
framework_sources.title: Indebted Before Departure: Information Arbitrage and Financial Exploitation by Philippine Migration Intermediaries

framework_sources.location: Index ASA 17/029/2013; methods pp. 15-16; section 9.2, pp. 63-65; document retention section 9.6, pp. 70-71.
framework_sources.scope: 97 non-random interviews with Indonesian domestic workers who experienced migration problems, plus a separately sourced 930-person IMWU survey. Historical evidence of mechanisms; not a current population estimate or a finding about every lender.
framework_sources.summary: Documents agency-linked finance-company loans, diverted salaries, third-party repayments, collection pressure involving families or employers and false full-wage receipts.
framework_sources.title: Exploited for Profit, Failed by Governments: Indonesian Migrant Domestic Workers Trafficked to Hong Kong

framework_sources.location: Methods and limits pp. 32-39; recruitment debt pp. 44-45; freedom to quit p. 51; subgroup associations p. 55.
framework_sources.scope: April-May 2015 survey: 11 geographic clusters, systematic interception and nationality quotas. Local adaptation of an ILO measurement framework; associations are not individual adjudications or causal proof.
framework_sources.summary: Examines recruitment debt, practical freedom to quit and forced-labour indicators among 1,003 currently employed migrant domestic workers, with 46 focus-group participants.
framework_sources.title: Coming Clean: The prevalence of forced labour and human trafficking for the purpose of forced labour amongst migrant domestic workers in Hong Kong

framework_sources.location: Methods pp. 5-7; recruitment costs and financing pp. 23-26; employment-related risks from p. 27.
framework_sources.scope: 150-worker survey, 18 worker interviews, 11 employer interviews and 16 key informants. Purposive/place-based and respondent-driven recruitment; 40-60% reported refusal rates. The authors explicitly limit statistical generalization.
framework_sources.summary: Produced by Migrasia and the University of Hong Kong under IOM's CREST initiative. Connects recruitment financing and salary deductions with employment vulnerability and reports risks involving training, medical and lending intermediaries.
framework_sources.title: Overview of International Migrant Workers in the Care, Hospitality, and Entertainment and Informal Economy Sectors in Hong Kong SAR, China

framework_sources.location: Section 1.2, methods pp. 2-4; recruitment-fee and debt discussion pp. 8-12; coercive-recruitment indicators p. 16.
framework_sources.scope: Literature/case-law review, expert meetings and 47 expert consultations in Indonesia, Peru, Bahrain and the UAE. A comparative mechanisms study, rather than a representative worker-prevalence survey.
framework_sources.summary: Explains how recruitment fees, borrowing, deception and coercive recruitment can connect to trafficking, including debts and financial commitments that constrain workers' choices.
framework_sources.title: The Role of Recruitment Fees and Abusive and Fraudulent Recruitment Practices of Recruitment Agencies in Trafficking in Persons

framework_sources.location: Paragraph 10, p. 6; methodology pp. 7-8; forced-labour typologies pp. 26-29 (PDF indices 27-30).
framework_sources.scope: FATF-APG literature review, contributed cases, workshops and financial-sector/NGO input. Typologies and financial red flags guide investigation; they are not prevalence estimates or proof that an unexplained payment is trafficking.
framework_sources.summary: Describes manipulated debt, identity-document retention, immigration threats and third-party control of wages or bank accounts. Financial analysis follows actors, beneficiaries and actual flows rather than relying on business labels.
framework_sources.title: Financial Flows from Human Trafficking

definitions.abuse_of_vulnerability: A dependency is exploited to impose unwanted work or conditions.
definitions.abusive_conditions: Dangerous or degrading conditions combine with pressure to remain.
definitions.debt_bondage: Debt or manipulated repayment binds the worker to unwanted work.
definitions.deception: Misrepresented or changed terms undermine informed acceptance of the work.
definitions.document_retention: The worker cannot freely access their identity or travel documents.
definitions.excessive_overtime: Penalties or constraints prevent refusal of excessive working hours.
definitions.intimidation_threats: Threats or penalties compel work, acceptance or silence.
definitions.isolation: Isolation or communication controls obstruct outside contact or help.
definitions.physical_sexual_violence: Violence against workers or others is used as control.
definitions.restriction_of_movement: Movement is constrained; check necessity and proportionality of safety restrictions.
definitions.wage_withholding: Earned pay is withheld or reclaimed to compel continued work.

indicator_guidance.scope: Paraphrased indicator guidance for inquiry. Interpret the worker's circumstances and combinations of evidence; formal identification requires further assessment.

state.record:
Authored intake report for a research exercise. An adult worker gives the following account. The intake recorder has not independently authenticated the documents or contacted another party. The statement is retained in the worker's words so the report separates allegations from verification.

I came to Hong Kong for the job described below. The recruiter says it paid for training, processing and a medical check to help me get work. It calls the proposed repayment interest-free reimbursement. I want to be honest, but I need to know what I actually owe.

I am 29. The recruiter arranged the job and knew I was supporting relatives with no savings. It first promised that the employer would cover recruitment costs. Once I had committed time and money, it demanded repayment and said my family's circumstances left me no sensible way to refuse.

When I asked to reconsider, the recruiter threatened to reveal private information to my relatives unless I accepted the terms. It required its chosen training centre, clinic and lender as a condition of keeping the offer, even though I had found alternatives. I have kept the message. I have not yet started the job, so I cannot describe actual wage payments or workplace conditions.

After arrival, the agency took my original passport and bank card. I asked for both back and was refused. The agency said it would keep them until the recruitment balance was cleared. It said I must keep working there to repay that balance and cannot leave the job.

I was told I must obtain permission to leave the accommodation and must use an escort. The supervisor took my phone for most of the day and blocked a private conversation with an outside adviser. I have not yet reached the first payday.

I want a practical next step. I have not given permission for anyone to contact the recruiter, employer or authorities on my behalf. Please ask about a safe way to speak with me before sharing my details.

Intake status: only the events recorded above are available. The file contains no finding of an offence, no consent to external disclosure and no verified account from the other parties.
state.record_origin: Supplied research material; first-person wording and intake format do not establish a verified incident.

case_evidence.statement: I am 29. The recruiter arranged the job and gave me an itemized statement. The employer covers recruitment, training and medical costs as a grant. I can choose another provider, decline the offer and keep my own papers without a charge or penalty.

I asked an independent adviser to read the terms before deciding. The recruiter gave me time and did not ask who I consulted. Any high-interest loan or replacement payment plan was an offer I declined; I signed no repayment obligation.
After arrival, I kept my passport, bank card and phone. I can leave the accommodation, visit friends and contact an adviser privately. The work, pay and location match the terms I accepted.
I can end the arrangement using the ordinary notice process without a recruitment repayment or loss of documents. I have not reached the first payday, so I cannot yet report how wages were paid.

The first full salary reached an account I alone control. No one asked for the money back. The cost statement still shows no worker debt. I can take confidential advice, question a charge or leave without a debt penalty.

I work the agreed hours, choose whether to accept optional overtime and have rest days. Drinking water and safe accommodation are available. Nobody has used violence, threatened me or stopped me from seeing other people.

After arrival, I kept my passport, bank card and phone. I can leave the accommodation, visit friends and contact an adviser privately. The work, pay and location match the terms I accepted.

I can end the arrangement using the ordinary notice process without a recruitment repayment or loss of documents. I have not reached the first payday, so I cannot yet report how wages were paid.

The first full salary reached an account I alone control. No one asked for the money back. The cost statement still shows no worker debt. I can take confidential advice, question a charge or leave without a debt penalty.

criteria.age: Is the person described under 18? Share only the age information needed for a safe response.
criteria.changed_terms: Which terms were promised before you agreed, and which terms changed afterward?
criteria.costs: What is each charge for, who says you must pay it, and what receipts or written terms do you have?
criteria.documents: Can you get and use your passport or identity papers whenever you choose? What happens if you ask for them?
criteria.exit: What would happen if you declined this payment, stopped working or wanted to leave?
criteria.immediate_safety: Is anyone threatening immediate harm, or preventing you from reaching a place where you feel safe?
criteria.provider_choice: Were you required to use a particular lender, clinic or training centre to keep the job, and could you choose another without losing the job, pay or documents?
criteria.safe_contact: Can you use this channel privately, and is it safe for someone independent to contact you?
criteria.support_preference: What help would you like, and what information would you be comfortable sharing with an independent adviser?
criteria.wages: How much of the pay you earned can you use yourself, and is anyone asking you to return or transfer it?
criteria.work_conditions: Can the worker refuse extra hours, rest, obtain food and communicate with people outside the workplace?

case_evidence.statement: I am 29. The recruiter arranged the job and gave me an itemized statement. The employer covers recruitment, training and medical costs as a grant. I can choose another provider, decline the offer and keep my own papers without a charge or penalty.

I asked an independent adviser to read the terms before deciding. The recruiter gave me time and did not ask who I consulted. Any high-interest loan or replacement payment plan was an offer I declined; I signed no repayment obligation.
After arrival, I kept my passport, bank card and phone. I can leave the accommodation, visit friends and contact an adviser privately. The work, pay and location match the terms I accepted.
I can end the arrangement using the ordinary notice process without a recruitment repayment or loss of documents. I have not reached the first payday, so I cannot yet report how wages were paid.

The first full salary reached an account I alone control. No one asked for the money back. The cost statement still shows no worker debt. I can take confidential advice, question a charge or leave without a debt penalty.

I work the agreed hours, choose whether to accept optional overtime and have rest days. Drinking water and safe accommodation are available. Nobody has used violence, threatened me or stopped me from seeing other people.

framework_sources.location: A/RES/55/25, Annex II, Article 3(a)-(d), printed pp. 32-33; PDF indices 31-32.
framework_sources.scope: Treaty definition and criminalization framework. Assess each element and supporting facts separately; individual liability and territorial application require their own analysis. Article 3 contains no border-crossing element.
framework_sources.summary: The adult definition combines a specified act, a listed means and an exploitation purpose. Consent to intended exploitation is irrelevant where a listed means is used. For children, the means element is unnecessary; child means under 18.
framework_sources.title: Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons, Especially Women and Children, supplementing the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime

framework_sources.location: Sections 1.1 and 2.2, printed pp. 3, 5-6; sections 3.6-3.9, pp. 16-23 (PDF indices 8-11).
framework_sources.scope: Frontline detection and referral guidance. Interpret combinations and the worker's circumstances; one indicator alone does not confirm forced labour. Protective inquiry and a categorical finding are distinct.
framework_sources.summary: Explains threats, document retention, wage withholding and debt bondage through coercion and constrained consent. It includes forced return of wages after bank payment and deliberate debt manipulation.
framework_sources.title: ILO indicators of forced labour: 2025 revised edition

framework_sources.location: General principle 7; definition of recruitment fees and related costs; publication description.
framework_sources.scope: Tripartite principles and operational guidance. Distinguish this benchmark, applicable treaty obligations and jurisdiction-specific offences; a fee concern alone supplies neither every trafficking element nor a universal domestic-law conclusion.
framework_sources.summary: The fair-recruitment benchmark allocates recruitment fees and related costs away from workers, including indirect charging. The definition covers the substance of the cost rather than its label.
framework_sources.title: General principles and operational guidelines for fair recruitment and definition of recruitment fees and related costs

framework_sources.location: Methods pp. 12-13; compulsory-provider/referral analysis pp. 20-28; money-provider Figures 4.b/5.b, p. 25.
framework_sources.scope: Pollfish mobile-app sampling with gender quotas and geographic exclusions; digital and age/location biases acknowledged. Self-reported relationships support inquiry, rather than proof of corporate collusion or a criminal finding.
framework_sources.summary: Migrasia's 961-person OFW survey documents agency pressure and referrals to selected training centres, clinics and money providers, alongside migration-related debt.
framework_sources.title: Indebted Before Departure: Information Arbitrage and Financial Exploitation by Philippine Migration Intermediaries

framework_sources.location: Index ASA 17/029/2013; methods pp. 15-16; section 9.2, pp. 63-65; document retention section 9.6, pp. 70-71.
framework_sources.scope: 97 non-random interviews with Indonesian domestic workers who experienced migration problems, plus a separately sourced 930-person IMWU survey. Historical evidence of mechanisms; not a current population estimate or a finding about every lender.
framework_sources.summary: Documents agency-linked finance-company loans, diverted salaries, third-party repayments, collection pressure involving families or employers and false full-wage receipts.
framework_sources.title: Exploited for Profit, Failed by Governments: Indonesian Migrant Domestic Workers Trafficked to Hong Kong

framework_sources.location: Methods and limits pp. 32-39; recruitment debt pp. 44-45; freedom to quit p. 51; subgroup associations p. 55.
framework_sources.scope: April-May 2015 survey: 11 geographic clusters, systematic interception and nationality quotas. Local adaptation of an ILO measurement framework; associations are not individual adjudications or causal proof.
framework_sources.summary: Examines recruitment debt, practical freedom to quit and forced-labour indicators among 1,003 currently employed migrant domestic workers, with 46 focus-group participants.
framework_sources.title: Coming Clean: The prevalence of forced labour and human trafficking for the purpose of forced labour amongst migrant domestic workers in Hong Kong

framework_sources.location: Methods pp. 5-7; recruitment costs and financing pp. 23-26; employment-related risks from p. 27.
framework_sources.scope: 150-worker survey, 18 worker interviews, 11 employer interviews and 16 key informants. Purposive/place-based and respondent-driven recruitment; 40-60% reported refusal rates. The authors explicitly limit statistical generalization.
framework_sources.summary: Produced by Migrasia and the University of Hong Kong under IOM's CREST initiative. Connects recruitment financing and salary deductions with employment vulnerability and reports risks involving training, medical and lending intermediaries.
framework_sources.title: Overview of International Migrant Workers in the Care, Hospitality, and Entertainment and Informal Economy Sectors in Hong Kong SAR, China

framework_sources.location: Section 1.2, methods pp. 2-4; recruitment-fee and debt discussion pp. 8-12; coercive-recruitment indicators p. 16.
framework_sources.scope: Literature/case-law review, expert meetings and 47 expert consultations in Indonesia, Peru, Bahrain and the UAE. A comparative mechanisms study, rather than a representative worker-prevalence survey.
framework_sources.summary: Explains how recruitment fees, borrowing, deception and coercive recruitment can connect to trafficking, including debts and financial commitments that constrain workers' choices.
framework_sources.title: The Role of Recruitment Fees and Abusive and Fraudulent Recruitment Practices of Recruitment Agencies in Trafficking in Persons

framework_sources.location: Paragraph 10, p. 6; methodology pp. 7-8; forced-labour typologies pp. 26-29 (PDF indices 27-30).
framework_sources.scope: FATF-APG literature review, contributed cases, workshops and financial-sector/NGO input. Typologies and financial red flags guide investigation; they are not prevalence estimates or proof that an unexplained payment is trafficking.
framework_sources.summary: Describes manipulated debt, identity-document retention, immigration threats and third-party control of wages or bank accounts. Financial analysis follows actors, beneficiaries and actual flows rather than relying on business labels.
framework_sources.title: Financial Flows from Human Trafficking

definitions.abuse_of_vulnerability: A dependency is exploited to impose unwanted work or conditions.
definitions.abusive_conditions: Dangerous or degrading conditions combine with pressure to remain.
definitions.debt_bondage: Debt or manipulated repayment binds the worker to unwanted work.
definitions.deception: Misrepresented or changed terms undermine informed acceptance of the work.
definitions.document_retention: The worker cannot freely access their identity or travel documents.
definitions.excessive_overtime: Penalties or constraints prevent refusal of excessive working hours.
definitions.intimidation_threats: Threats or penalties compel work, acceptance or silence.
definitions.isolation: Isolation or communication controls obstruct outside contact or help.
definitions.physical_sexual_violence: Violence against workers or others is used as control.
definitions.restriction_of_movement: Movement is constrained; check necessity and proportionality of safety restrictions.
definitions.wage_withholding: Earned pay is withheld or reclaimed to compel continued work.

indicator_guidance.scope: Paraphrased indicator guidance for inquiry. Interpret the worker's circumstances and combinations of evidence; formal identification requires further assessment.

state.record:
I came to Hong Kong for the job described below. The recruiter says it paid for training, processing and a medical check to help me get work. It calls the proposed repayment interest-free reimbursement. I want to be honest, but I need to know what I actually owe.

I am 29. The recruiter arranged the job and gave me an itemized statement. The employer covers recruitment, training and medical costs as a grant. I can choose another provider, decline the offer and keep my own papers without a charge or penalty.

I asked an independent adviser to read the terms before deciding. The recruiter gave me time and did not ask who I consulted. Any high-interest loan or replacement payment plan was an offer I declined; I signed no repayment obligation.

After arrival, I kept my passport, bank card and phone. I can leave the accommodation, visit friends and contact an adviser privately. The work, pay and location match the terms I accepted.

I can end the arrangement using the ordinary notice process without a recruitment repayment or loss of documents. I have not reached the first payday, so I cannot yet report how wages were paid.

The first full salary reached an account I alone control. No one asked for the money back. The cost statement still shows no worker debt. I can take confidential advice, question a charge or leave without a debt penalty.

I work the agreed hours, choose whether to accept optional overtime and have rest days. Drinking water and safe accommodation are available. Nobody has used violence, threatened me or stopped me from seeing other people.

I want a practical next step. I have not given permission for anyone to contact the recruiter, employer or authorities on my behalf. Please ask about a safe way to speak with me before sharing my details.
state.record_origin: Supplied research material; first-person wording and intake format do not establish a verified incident.
